o: We must scan a string and replace exact HTML entities (`"`, `'`, `&`, `>`, `<`, `⁄`) with their characters. The key subtlety: a `&` only starts an entity if it is followed by one of these exact sequences; otherwise it stays literal (e.g. `&ambassador;` is untouched). Also, replacements happen on the original text, so order of replacement matters if done naively — e.g. replacing `&` first then scanning again could double-process text produced by earlier replacements. With length up to $10^5$, any linear or near-linear scan works; quadratic repeated passes over the whole string are still fine in practice but a single pass is cleanest.
k: An entity starts at '&' but only counts if the immediately following characters exactly match one of the six known entities.
Replacements must be based on the original string, not re-scanned output, to avoid cascading replacements like '&amp;' → '&' → '&'.
A single left-to-right scan checking each candidate entity at each '&' gives O(n) time.

a.i: The most intuitive idea: for each entity, call the language's built-in replace-all on the whole string, from longest/most specific to shortest. Replacing `&` last would be wrong because earlier replacements could create new `&` patterns? Actually here no replacement output contains another entity's full pattern except that `&` outputs could combine with later text — so we replace `&` FIRST, then the others; since none of the other entities' outputs contain `&`, subsequent passes cannot create new valid entities. This relies on careful ordering and is simple but does multiple full-string passes.
s: Replace all occurrences of `&` with `&` first.
a.t: O(6 * n * L) worst case where L is average entity length (~6), effectively O(n) per pass, 6 passes total — linear in practice.
a.sp: O(n) for the output string copies.

a.n: Approach 2: Single-Pass Scan with Hash Map (Optimal)
a.i: Walk through the string once. Whenever we see `&`, try to match the next up-to-7 characters against the six known entities stored in a hash map keyed by entity string. If a match is found, append the mapped character and jump past the entity; otherwise append `&` literally and move one step. This guarantees each character of the input is examined a constant number of times and never re-processes replaced output.
s: Build a map from each entity string to its replacement character.
Iterate index i over the text; if text[i] != '&', append it and advance.
If text[i] == '&', check substrings of lengths 4–7 starting at i against the map (longest match wins).
On a match, append the mapped char and set i += matched length; otherwise append '&' and i += 1.
a.t: O(n) — each position is visited once; at each '&' at most 4 constant-length substring lookups.

w: In an interview, present Approach 2: it demonstrates you understand that replacements must be anchored to the original text and runs in a single pass. Approach 1 is acceptable as a quick solution but invites discussion about replacement ordering pitfalls. Common pitfalls: forgetting that unmatched '&' (like in '&ambassador;') must be kept verbatim; replacing '&' last causing cascaded substitutions; off-by-one errors when slicing near the end of the string. Edge cases: text that is entirely one entity, multiple adjacent entities ('&&&'), and '&' at the very end of the string. Follow-ups might ask how to handle arbitrary HTML entities (use a trie or regex with a dictionary) or streaming input (buffer up to max entity length before deciding).
